Author: @terabyte994
Content:
when you try searching a youtube video and you see "Explore more".
At its core, the "Explore More" tab functions as a digital curator. Unlike the standard recommendation feed, which leans heavily on viewing history and algorithms fine-tuned to past behavior, the “Explore” tab offers something richer: diversity and intentional discovery. It highlights trending topics, emerging creators, and popular videos across categories that users may not have previously engaged with — from science and technology to travel, fashion, gaming, and global news.

This element of serendipity is crucial. While algorithm-based suggestions tend to create echo chambers — reinforcing existing preferences — the “Explore” section challenges viewers to step outside their bubble. It fosters intellectual curiosity, broadens perspectives, and introduces voices that might otherwise be buried beneath YouTube’s sheer volume of content.

Moreover, for new or smaller creators, the “Explore More” tab is a golden opportunity. It levels the playing field by offering visibility outside the strict bounds of subscriber counts and search metrics. It amplifies content based on quality and relevance rather than popularity alone, thereby nurturing a more vibrant and inclusive creative ecosystem.

From a user-experience standpoint, the “Explore More” tab also promotes balance. It offers a reprieve from the endless scroll of personalized videos by organizing content into themes and interests. It transforms passive consumption into an active journey of exploration — akin to browsing curated shelves in a library rather than being handed a stack of already-read books.

In conclusion, the “Explore More” tab is far more than an optional feature — it’s a necessary tool in navigating the digital labyrinth of modern media. It empowers users to discover the unfamiliar, encourages thoughtful engagement, and fosters a dynamic, diverse content environment. In a platform as immense and influential as YouTube, this kind of structured discovery isn’t just helpful — it’s essential.

There's something that google has been doing lately that people in the US, or other English speaking countries, might not realize (since most of the internet is in English).

This is slow, almost always completely breaks the website, is very intrusive and it probably steals your data. I HATE IT.
IF I SEARCH FOR SOMETHING IN ENGLISH ITS BECAUSE I SPEAK ENGLISH, STOP TRYING TO TRANSLATE EVERYTHING WHILE FAILING TO DO SO.

Also, I assume google probably does this too whenever there's a mismatch between the search results and your system language, or it might even use your location too, since i changed my phone's system language and it still does that. Author: @TehShadowDeath
Content:
What if Google is actively destroying its search results in an effort to get people to use Gemini instead? I mean I used to think Google butchered their search results so that people would keep searching by rephrasing what they're looking for to try and find better results. Each time you search they put ads at the top of that page.

I mean, Google sells ads. Historically you would search for something on Google, then go to a site in the search results and see ads on that site provided by Google. Then Google started putting ads in the search results. Now, by pushing people to Gemini they can push ads without you going to a 3rd party site and Google having to pay them for the ads.. Aaaaaand you stay on their site as you continue to search more. It really just seems like they're trying to make their site the one stop shop so you never leave their site.

Author: @DavidJBurbridge
Content:
Google doesn't fully support basic search operators any more. It used to be that I could wrap double quotation marks and it would show only the pages with that precise phrase. Now? It will often skip many pages that I know contain that phrase (and not obscure ones) or include pages that lack the phrase entirely. Also it often ignores the minus sign operator. It's like it only does what you want based on some obscure rule set. 
I asked ChatGPT to find me an article I read a long time ago. It did a better job of hunting it down than Google did. An LLM with search as an afterthought did better than the king of Internet search. 
If you weren't online in the 2000s, you won't remember how much better Google was back then. If something wasn't on Google, chances are it didn't exist on the clear web.

Author: @Gnurklesquimp2
Content:
I never go out of my way to use AI, if I need to know where the latest version of windows hid a setting I still just google it. The AI results that have come up for that kinda thing are more convenient than delving into bloated articles that want you to consent to their cookies etc., but we had the quick list where you could expand questions and their answers google fetched from sites, and that basically did the same job. 

I hate every search engine (Or at least what it has to deal with) I've used nowadays, best bet is to try several in my experience.
Good AI to help us navigate what people are saying instead of having it just hallucinate what it thinks people are saying seems vital... Let it merely hallucinate what it thinks we wanna find, cause it'll probably still be better than rolling the slot machine that manual searching currently is. However. that's not really a solution when the ''real'' articles etc. it'll link us to are themselves AI attempts at truth, at best.

If such an AI would detect and filter out AI bs cause it recognizes the patterns, that'd potentially help with the downside of false positives, but I'm guessing the catch-22 is that the then updated AI creating the bs will improve to be just as realistic as the detection can make out, even whenever it is the detection that improves first... Meaning it's accelerating the problem and potentially getting us into hotter water less prepared.
It's almost like a virus in that way, fight it and it might just get stronger faster.

8:30 And ohh god yes the feedback loop is probably gonna get out of hand. Let's just hope it breaks altogether and the occasional real human thing is easy to tell apart? It's so hard to picture what it may spiral into.

The only counter argument is that LLMs are WILDLY inefficient in terms of resources used to achieve a search result.

They are dangerously deceptive; we don’t see their impact, so we might just use it as we would a regular google search, but somewhere out there is a data center with racks of screaming hot computers trying to crunch all these LLM requests - the climate emissions are awful, the power consumption is abysmal, and it (the searches) could all be achieved for much less with a little patience and a few more seconds of time.

Author: @HuiHaiZ
Content:
How to get 'rid' of the "AI Overview" slop (At least in Chrome on PC idk about other browsers/Mobile)

- Got to browser settings
- Search engine
- Manage search engines and site search
- Click 'Add' button next to "Site Search"

- Name (what ever you want, i named mine 'No AI slop' lol)
- Shortcut (i don't think it matters, maybe if you use some sort of shortcut it might, not sure)
- URL "{google:baseURL}search?q=%s&udm=14" (without " " obv) this is important, it makes your search "web" searches instead of the normal "all" searches thus not showing the AI slop
- Then press 3 dots and make default

Technically this does not disable/ or get rid of the AI slop just makes it different search option (and imo its way better too) and you can still see the slop if you use the "all" option in searches.
Additionally there is likely way to block the Ai slop with other means too but haven't looked into it.

Lastly i found this some time ago in some Reddit post but couldn't find that post/ comment, but i hope this helps someone as it did help me :)
